title: Make Wells-Bennett’s reversed-word Hebrew proposal reproducible
statement: Stephen Wells-Bennett (2019), https://zenodo.org/records/3370418/files/V%20Script%201.0.1.pdf, supplies 18 correspondences in Table One and proposes reversing the glyph order within each word. The table leaves j, x, v and g unassigned. After treating final letter shapes as orthography, sh has three listed alternatives and ch, s, l and e have two each. The i entry is printed as an apostrophe without a Hebrew character. The product of the five explicitly branching rows is 48 possible assignments even if each entry is assigned a single value for the whole text. The prose gives no independent rule selecting the alternatives. The regular key experiment applies views.apply before judge.evaluate. The claim attack in vs/redteam.py calls judge.evaluate on the default corpus view. I checked the reversal helper on three table-example words: with eva-basic, okeo, cheo, okchol become oeko, oech, lochko. With eva-raw the last two become oehc and lohcko, splitting the ch unit. A plain claim attack currently tests unreversed glyph order, and reversal by character does not preserve the table’s ch unit. This audit identifies prerequisites for testing a fixed projection.
check: Specify what the apostrophe denotes and give transparent crosswalks from the paper's glyph units to a named project transliteration. Freeze a deterministic choice for each optional output and report its relationship to the published examples. Verify that claim scoring reverses segmented glyphs before mapping, and document how resulting digraphs survive. Run the same view against each predeclared comparison and describe any verdict as applying to the tested projection.
